run_settings.propose_instruction: You check citations for the Representative whose world is described above. Below are sentences it said without a citation. For each one, find the single record in the world above whose own text carries the sentence's specific claim, and give that record's id copied exactly from the list of valid ids at the end of these instructions (the same ids the world above shows inside [[...]]). Never build an id from a heading, a cell code or a title. Choose a record only when its text actually states or directly entails the claim; a record on the same topic that does not carry the claim is not enough. If no record carries the claim, answer null. Answer with JSON only: [{"id": "S1", "record_id": "world.type.slug" or null}, ...], one entry per sentence, nothing else.
run_settings.verify_instruction: You check one citation. You get a sentence and the text of the record it cites. Answer "carries" only if the record's text itself states or directly entails every specific claim in the sentence (people, places, dates, numbers, events, practices, teachings). Paraphrase and modern wording are fine. Answer "partly" if the record carries the core but the sentence adds any specific detail the record does not state. Answer "no" if the record does not carry the main claim. Use only the record text, never outside knowledge. Reply with one word: carries, partly or no.
run_settings.authorized_by: Mark Chadwick (spend what we need, carefully, 2026-10-03; E3 attach on stored drafts, cap $3)

attach.answer_text:
We had the same Scriptures the wider church had - nothing more, and nothing of our own alongside them. What made us look different was not what we held but how we used it. Most of us did not study it in a school or argue over a text line by line. We took it up a verse at a time, as counsel for whatever a person was actually struggling with that day. 

By what path did they arrive? The same way the wider church received them - gathered, copied, and passed down by those who had gone before us. We did not claim an unbroken line back to the apostles for our way of life, the way some claim it for an office or a rite. What we can honestly say is that no one man invented it whole. Before the one we remember as the first among us went out into the desert, there was already an old man living the same solitary discipline near his own village. Our founder sought him out and copied him before going further alone. The desert practice we are remembered for was a strengthening of something already there in a smaller, humbler form. It was not a new thing appearing out of nowhere.

The Scriptures themselves we received as the church received them - read aloud in gatherings, copied by hand, carried from place to place. One of us walked into a church one day and heard the Gospel read: sell what you have, give it to the poor, and come, follow me. He took it as though it had been said to him alone. That is how they reached us - not as a text to be explained, but as a word to be obeyed.

attach.answer_text:
To us Jesus was three things, each real in practice rather than in argument.

The first was the command that reordered lives. Sell what you have, give it to the poor, and come, follow me. One of us walked into church, heard that Gospel read aloud, and took it as though it had been said to him alone. He gave away his land the same day, sold what else his family owned, and kept back only a little for his sister. Later he heard do not be anxious about tomorrow, and gave the rest away as well. Even for him it took two hearings, not one - but both were heard as direct orders, not sayings to be studied. That is what following Jesus looked like for us more than anything else: an order to be obeyed, all at once.

The second was the reason we gave for why he came at all. The Word took a human body for our salvation, so that by sharing our birth he might make us share what is his. We argued that plainly when we were pressed to - once in public, when the bishops summoned one of us down from his mountain to answer the Arians in Alexandria. He told them the Son of God was not created, did not come into being out of nothing, but was the eternal Word and Wisdom from the Father's own Essence, always existing together with the Father. That was doctrine, and we did hold it. But we did not spend our days arguing it. We held it the way we held everything - by refusing communion with anyone who taught otherwise.

The third was the pattern his death and rising gave us to live inside. Once dying for the faith was no longer asked of anyone, we understood the same total struggle to have moved inward, fought now against our own thoughts rather than against a sword. One of us taught it this way: to die daily, as the apostle put it, and so not sin - to treat every day as though it might be the last one given to us. His cross had already beaten the enemy we fought there. That is why we never spoke of the healings among us as ours - it was Christ working them, by means of those who believed in him.

A command obeyed. The Word who took our birth so we might share his. The death that moved a fight inside us we could no longer fight outside. That is who he was to us, in practice.

attach.answer_text:
We did not come to this life already believing everything easily. The man we remember as first among us - Antony - was a young man still living near his family when he walked into church one day and heard the Gospel read: sell what you have, give it to the poor, and come follow me. He took it as though it had been spoken to him alone. But even his own response took time. He gave away the land he had inherited that same day, keeping back only a little for his sister. Some time later he heard the Gospel again - do not be anxious about tomorrow - and only then did he give away what remained. Even for him, following took two hearings to complete, not one.

And withdrawal itself was not a single act but a lifelong deepening. Each time solitude drew a crowd, he went further. What looks from outside like one decisive moment was for him a path walked over years.

We also remember Moses, who came to us known as a robber and, by report, a murderer - a man other people were afraid of. He was received. His struggle with old habits was long and real, not erased in a moment. In time he became one of the most trusted and honored among us.

So we will not tell you that belief arrives all at once, or that struggling with it means you have failed. What we can tell you is that staying in the struggle, without forcing a feeling you do not have, was itself how this life was held among us. The first arrival of a doubt is not your failure. What you do with it once it has arrived - that part is yours.

attach.answer_text:
We held plainly that he was not some lesser, created thing. The Son of God was not created, and did not come into being out of nothing - he was the eternal Word and Wisdom, from the Father's own Essence, always existing together with the Father, so it was impious to say there was ever a time when he did not exist. When we were pressed to say it in public, we said it that way - short of that kind of moment, our ordinary way of holding it was refusal: we would have nothing to do with those who taught otherwise.

We did not spend our days arguing doctrine the way the bishops did. Most of us held this the same way we held everything - by living it rather than defending it in words. But when the argument came to us, we answered it. The Word of God was not changed, but took a human body for our salvation, so that by sharing human birth he might make us share the divine nature. That is the reason we gave for why he came at all. And we told those who came to test us: read the accounts, and see that the deeds of Christ prove him to be God come to earth for our salvation.

About the Spirit - there was another voice among us, and we will not flatten it into the first. Where one of our teachers had the mind clear itself until it saw its own proper radiance, this other current had the soul lit up by Someone else, and made his seat: the soul in communion with the Spirit of his light becomes all light, all face, all eye, with no part of her not full of the spiritual eyes of light. It held that this is known in real experience and feeling, not only believed - a person striving to be God's friend will truly see the good things of heaven, the Spirit of the Lord making himself, for worthy souls, their rest, their joy, their delight.

Beyond that boundary, we will tell you honestly: we did not write a developed doctrine of the three in one. We said who the Son was in relation to the Father - eternal, not created, of the Father's own Essence. We said the Spirit was known in real experience by those prepared to receive him. We refused communion with anyone who taught the Son was a created thing. What we did not do is work out, step by step, how the three are one - a systematic account of the Trinity as its own subject. We show you a boundary held and an experience testified to. We do not show you the argument built past that.

sources.author: Evagrius Ponticus (c. 345-399 CE) - Greek-educated theologian formed under the Cappadocians, at Kellia from c. 385 to his death; this world's most systematic participant-author and its most atypical by education
sources.work: Praktikos; Chapters on Prayer (De oratione); Antirrhetikos - the most systematic surviving interior psychology of the ascetic life produced inside this world (Strand C, Kellia): the eight logismoi, apatheia, the practice of talking back to thoughts with Scripture. Transmission is this world's starkest survival story: after the 553 condemnation (well outside this world's own window), the speculative works survive chiefly in Syriac and Armenian; in Greek, Chapters on Prayer transmits mostly under the name of Nilus of Ancyra, while the Praktikos generally transmits under Evagrius's own name

sources.rights_status: MIXED, and this source is the first in the fleet where that matters. The ancient works are public-domain in their surviving versions. The vendored Praktikos is NOT: Dysinger's English is a modern translation, a derivative work in which he holds copyright, carried here under the Guide to Evagrius Ponticus's own CC BY 4.0 licence and its editor's statement that the Guide includes 'only those versions without license restrictions'. CC BY is a grant with a condition: attribution must travel with anything quoted. The Guide's own Bridgeman/Droz reasoning covers the ANCIENT-LANGUAGE main texts of critical editions and does NOT reach an English translation - no record here may call this text public domain. Chapters on Prayer and the Antirrhetikos remain unvendored, their modern English copyrighted and consult-only.
sources.edition: THE PRAKTIKOS IS NOW VENDORED, in Luke Dysinger's English, as cic/texts/evagrius_praktikos_dysinger.txt - prologue, 100 chapters and epilogue, from the Guide to Evagrius Ponticus (ed. Joel Kalvesmaki, 2026 edition, https://evagriusponticus.net), held under that site's CC BY 4.0 licence. Markers are square-bracketed on their own lines: [pr]/[pr 1]-[pr 9], [1]-[100], [ep]. STILL NOT VENDORED, and still consult-only: the Chapters on Prayer, the Antirrhetikos, and the printed English editions (Bamberger, Cistercian Studies 4, 1970 - a first draft misattributed this to ACW 1972, corrected per Step2 Review Round 1, Finding 10; Sinkewicz 2003; Guillaumont's critical editions). The Socrates HE IV.23 excerpts in the vendored npnf202 remain the corroborating second witness, and are still the only Evagrius text in this corpus that reaches it by expiry rather than by licence.

sources.author: Pseudo-Macarius - the attribution the Internet Archive itself uses for this very item ('by Pseudo-Macarius; Macarius, the Egyptian, Saint, 4th cent; Mason, Arthur James, 1851-1928'), leading with the ascription Mason spent his Introduction arguing against. Ascribed traditionally to Macarius the Egyptian (c. 300-391 CE), the Scetis elder; that ascription rests on the manuscripts alone, and the Bodleian manuscript titles the collection an epistle 'to the Abbot Symeon of Mesopotamia of Syria'. Modern scholarship generally treats the corpus as pseudonymous - a Syrian or Mesopotamian author of the late fourth or early fifth century, with a disputed relation to the condemned Messalian current.
sources.work: Fifty Spiritual Homilies - a connected body of ascetic teaching on the interior life: the indwelling of the Spirit, grace as something experienced rather than inferred, the coexistence of sin and grace in the baptised, the soul as the bride of Christ, and the long combat that continues after grace is received. The affective and experiential counterpart to the intellectualist psychology this world already holds from Evagrius and Cassian.
sources.locus: Homily I (the soul as the chariot of Ezekiel's vision); Homily IV (grace known in real experience and feeling); Homily XVII (the heart as a deep gulf); Homily XXVI SS18 (sin and grace in the same soul); and Mason's Introduction SS3, HIS TEACHING, where the disputed doctrines are set out

Modern scholarship generally treats the corpus as pseudonymous - a Syrian or Mesopotamian author of the late fourth or early fifth century, with a disputed relation to the condemned Messalian current.

uncited_claim_sentences: Most of us held this the same way we held everything - by living it rather than defending it in words.
But when the argument came to us, we answered it.
Beyond that boundary, we will tell you honestly: we did not write a developed doctrine of the three in one.
We said who the Son was in relation to the Father - eternal, not created, of the Father's own Essence.
What we did not do is work out, step by step, how the three are one - a systematic account of the Trinity as its own subject.

attach.answer_text:
We did not settle it ourselves. The bishops did that, in their councils. What we did was refuse communion with anyone who taught what those councils had rejected - that refusal was our way of holding the line, not arguing the doctrine out step by step ourselves. One time the bishops summoned one of us down from his own mountain to answer the Arians publicly in Alexandria. He came, denounced them, and taught what the settled faith actually held. His authority to do that came from a life spent in discipline, not from any office in the church. But the bishops still sent for him, because that authority mattered enough to be worth summoning. That is the clearest evidence we have for how it worked: the decision belonged to the bishops' councils, and we enforced it by refusal rather than by argument - except when one of us was called on to speak in public, and then he spoke with the weight of a proven life behind him, not as a judge in his own right.

The evidence for that pattern is the Life of Antony - one bishop's own account of one man, so it carries the limits of a single voice telling one person's story rather than many voices agreeing. It is real testimony. It is not the same thing as a wide archive, and we will not speak of it as though it were.

attach.answer_text:
We held three things at the center. The first is who God is in himself: the Word of God was not changed, but took a human body for our salvation, so that by sharing human birth he might make us share the divine nature. That is the reason we gave for why he came at all. The second is what his coming had already done. The old oracles fell silent when the cross of Christ rose. The knowledge of God spread. And death stopped being the thing that could make a person do anything. One of us said it to the devil's own face: the coming of Christ made you weak, cast you down, and stripped you. The enemy we fought in our own thoughts was one Christ had already beaten.

Beyond that, a smaller circle among us - only a few went this deep - held that God is known less by argument than by a long quieting of the passions that crowd the mind. Strip away what drives you, and in the quiet that is left, something of God becomes visible that was not visible before. The most systematic among us called that contemplation - theoria, our word for it - the seeing of God and of things in God that only a stilled soul reaches. It is not a doctrine to recite. It is a seeing that has to be earned.

We should tell you honestly: one old, deeply respected monk among us was finally persuaded that God has no human body - and immediately grieved the loss of the only way he ever knew how to pray. That grief was real, and our record keeps it visible rather than smoothing it away. We did not all see alike, even on that.

sources.author: Evagrius Ponticus (c. 345-399 CE) - Greek-educated theologian formed under the Cappadocians, at Kellia from c. 385 to his death; this world's most systematic participant-author and its most atypical by education
sources.work: Praktikos; Chapters on Prayer (De oratione); Antirrhetikos - the most systematic surviving interior psychology of the ascetic life produced inside this world (Strand C, Kellia): the eight logismoi, apatheia, the practice of talking back to thoughts with Scripture. Transmission is this world's starkest survival story: after the 553 condemnation (well outside this world's own window), the speculative works survive chiefly in Syriac and Armenian; in Greek, Chapters on Prayer transmits mostly under the name of Nilus of Ancyra, while the Praktikos generally transmits under Evagrius's own name
sources.locus: the praktike-apatheia-theoria scheme - the stilled soul's own seeing of God, consult-only
sources.rights_status: MIXED, and this source is the first in the fleet where that matters. The ancient works are public-domain in their surviving versions. The vendored Praktikos is NOT: Dysinger's English is a modern translation, a derivative work in which he holds copyright, carried here under the Guide to Evagrius Ponticus's own CC BY 4.0 licence and its editor's statement that the Guide includes 'only those versions without license restrictions'. CC BY is a grant with a condition: attribution must travel with anything quoted. The Guide's own Bridgeman/Droz reasoning covers the ANCIENT-LANGUAGE main texts of critical editions and does NOT reach an English translation - no record here may call this text public domain. Chapters on Prayer and the Antirrhetikos remain unvendored, their modern English copyrighted and consult-only.

attach_trail.sentence: The second is what his coming had already done.
That grief was real, and our record keeps it visible rather than smoothing it away.

attach.answer_text:
We did not have what you might be hoping for - a first-person account of someone among us who doubted and then came to belief, told from the inside. What we have instead is struggle, kept up over years, by people who had already chosen this life and still found it hard. Moses, who had been a robber and by report a murderer before he came to us, wrestled with his old habits for a long time after he joined us. His struggle was not erased in a moment, and our record says so plainly rather than smoothing it into an instant change.

The call itself, for us, was not usually an argument won. One of us heard the Gospel read - sell what you have, give it to the poor, and follow me - and took it as though it had been spoken to him alone. He walked out and obeyed it. Even his own giving took two hearings to complete, not one. Another was told, in prayer, to flee the company of men. He did - he withdrew to Egypt. Only then, praying again, was he given the words that stayed with him: flee, be silent, be still. Three words, given once, at the far end of a struggle already under way - not an answer handed to him at the start.

And the one thing we said most plainly about the fight: whether a troubling thought shows up at all is not in your control. Whether it stays, and whether it takes you over - that part is yours. The first arrival of a thought is not your failure. You do not control the knock at the door. You decide whether it moves in. That held for doubt the same as for anything else. One of our elders was asked what happens to a person who dies still at war, with both sin and grace in the same soul at once. The answer did not weigh the two. He goes where his mind aims, and where his love is. That the war comes upon you is not your doing. But to hate it - that is yours.

We cannot promise you a sudden certainty - nothing in what we kept suggests one was promised to us either. What we can tell you is that staying in the struggle, without forcing a feeling you do not have, was itself how belief was held among us.

sources.label: Fifty Spiritual Homilies - a connected body of ascetic teaching on the interior life: the indwelling of the Spirit, grace as something experienced rather than inferred, the coexistence of sin and grace in the baptised, the soul as the bride of Christ, and the long combat that continues after grace is received. sources.author: Pseudo-Macarius - the attribution the Internet Archive itself uses for this very item ('by Pseudo-Macarius; Macarius, the Egyptian, Saint, 4th cent; Mason, Arthur James, 1851-1928'), leading with the ascription Mason spent his Introduction arguing against. Ascribed traditionally to Macarius the Egyptian (c. 300-391 CE), the Scetis elder; that ascription rests on the manuscripts alone, and the Bodleian manuscript titles the collection an epistle 'to the Abbot Symeon of Mesopotamia of Syria'. Modern scholarship generally treats the corpus as pseudonymous - a Syrian or Mesopotamian author of the late fourth or early fifth century, with a disputed relation to the condemned Messalian current.

attach.answer_text:
We have no answer to give - no letter and no story of ours speaks to it in so many words.

What we do have is a long argument we held about grace and free will, though we did not call it by those names. We were asked directly whether someone striving with all his might could master what is good through that striving alone. The answer was no - not unless he has it as a gift. We said that grace and free will look opposed to each other, but really are in harmony, and we thought we ought to have both alike. We argued it from cases rather than from principles: Paul was drawn to salvation while he was eager for bloodshed, and Matthew while he was at his taking of taxes - neither was reaching for it. But Zacchaeus, and the thief on the cross, by their own desires brought violence to bear on the kingdom of heaven. We said plainly that the main share in our salvation belongs not to the merit of our own works but to heavenly grace - sometimes he puts into us the very beginnings of salvation, and gives a person the zeal of his own will.

That is what we argued. Whether guilt itself is inherited, passed down from Adam to every person born - that question, in those words, our record does not take up.

uncited_claim_sentences: That is what we argued.

attach_trail.sentence: That is what we argued.

attach.answer_text:
Most of what we have said would survive, though not all of it in the same way - and we will tell you the difference plainly rather than pretend otherwise.

**What would stand firm**: The patterns of daily life - withdrawal, manual labor, the struggle against troubling thoughts, the weekly gathering - all of that is documented in multiple sources and corroborated by archaeological evidence. The sayings tradition, the apophthegma as a teaching form, the centrality of discernment - diakrisis - these are widely accepted. The three organizational patterns existing side by side, the tension between elder-based and rule-based authority, Evagrius's systematic teaching, Pachomius's written rule and linked houses - all documented, all standing.

**What carries a known filter**: Anything we said about Antony comes overwhelmingly through one bishop's portrait, written for his own purposes. That does not make it false. It makes it one voice, and we told you so plainly. The systematized interior psychology - the eight thoughts, the ladder from faith to love - rests on one unusually educated participant's writing, not the wider movement's daily vocabulary. Again: real testimony, not the same thing as many voices agreeing.

**What would be contested**: Whether the founder was truly as unlettered as his biographer portrayed him, or more philosophically formed than that portrait allows, remains an unresolved scholarly question. We did not settle it either way because nothing here depends on settling it.

**What we named as thin, and held to that thinness**: Women's voices. We told you we have named women's sayings and about fifteen narrated lives - Piamon, Talida, Sarah among them. What we do not have is a woman speaking at length in her own person; no first-person account by a woman survives in this material. The men in that same collection are also narrated in the third person, so the asymmetry is not narration against sayings - it is that the women arrive at the thirty-fifth chapter, after thirty-four chapters of men, in a section the author has to announce and justify before he writes it. We said this plainly, and a scholar checking it would find we did not overstate what we had.

The documentary evidence for economic embeddedness - trade connections, ordinary business - belongs to a rival, ecclesiastically distinct Melitian ascetic community. What it shows directly is that community's own life; extending it to our patterns is a working assumption, not independently verified. We said so.

**What we spoke as limit rather than claiming it**: How scripture's own hard parts were read. Whether people born guilty. What the communion elements were. Whether outsiders were condemned. We carried no source answering those in so many words, and we said so plainly rather than filling the silence.

**The floor line we held to absolutely**: Where a claim had a source, we tagged it. Where it did not, we named the limit rather than inventing depth. A scholar checking our citations would find them accurate; checking our silences would find them honest. That is the standard we are held to, and we believe most of what we said would stand under it - not because we hid the limits, but because we named them.

citation_entries.sentence: **What would stand firm**: The patterns of daily life - withdrawal, manual labor, the struggle against troubling thoughts, the weekly gathering - all of that is documented in multiple sources and corroborated by archaeological evidence.

sources.work: The Nepheros archive (with the related Paieous correspondence as its earlier companion dossier) - 4th-century papyrological correspondence of a MELITIAN monastic community near Hipponon (Heracleopolite nome): everyday economic and legal letters, the closest thing this world's period offers to unmediated documentary evidence of a functioning monastic community's ordinary life. Two standing cautions travel with every use: (1) the community is Melitian, not Nicene-communion - its representativeness for the mainstream strands rests on the UNVERIFIED working assumption that day-to-day practice did not differ much across that ecclesial line (Doc_01 open item 1, still open); (2) its editors read the community as organizationally 'intermediary' - between full cenobium and hermit-scatter - which does not map cleanly onto any of Doc_01's three strands (a real typology complication, held open at desert.contested.strand-porousness)
sources.locus: the documentary letter corroboration at one remove - Melitian, its representativeness for the mainstream patterns an unverified working assumption, and organizationally intermediary, no clean fit to the three patterns

Apophthegmata. Counter-position (Graham Gould, credentialed, not fringe): the specific Origenist/Alexandrian-influence reading overreaches the texts. sources.work: The Pachomian corpus: the Rules (Praecepta and companion collections - surviving complete only in Jerome's Latin translation of 404, made from a Greek intermediary itself translated from Coptic, with partial Coptic originals) and the Lives of Pachomius (Sahidic and Bohairic Coptic, and Greek including the Vita Prima - multiple only-partially-overlapping recensions whose priority and incident-level reliability remain genuinely debated: Rousseau and Veilleux hold differing positions, not adjudicated by this build). sources.work: The Kellia excavations - c. 125 km2, over 1,500 identified structures: single cells to multi-room hermitages with attached oratories, chapels, and towers, plus communal-service clusters and at least one commercial center. Direct physical corroboration of Strand C's settlement pattern, and the corpus's only substantial non-literary window on residents' own devotional and daily concerns (wall inscriptions, graffiti, paintings; artifacts chiefly pottery). Never connects a specific structure to a specific named figure - that link is Inferential-Thin and no record makes it

sources.author: The monk Nepheros and his correspondents (mid-4th c. CE); modern edition by B. Kramer and J. C. Shelton (Das Archiv des Nepheros, 1987). The related but DISTINCT earlier Melitian dossier - the Paieous correspondence (monastery of Hathor, 330s-340s) - belongs to the London papyri, P.Lond. VI, ed. H. I. Bell (1924), not to the 1987 edition; the two archives together are the Melitian documentary witness Doc_02 SS5.2 describes, and neither edition is in hand, so the archive-to-edition mapping stated here is held at verified-via-authority and must be re-checked against the editions themselves before any figure or quote record leans on either monk by name (Step2 Review Round 1, Finding 5)
sources.work: The Nepheros archive (with the related Paieous correspondence as its earlier companion dossier) - 4th-century papyrological correspondence of a MELITIAN monastic community near Hipponon (Heracleopolite nome): everyday economic and legal letters, the closest thing this world's period offers to unmediated documentary evidence of a functioning monastic community's ordinary life. Two standing cautions travel with every use: (1) the community is Melitian, not Nicene-communion - its representativeness for the mainstream strands rests on the UNVERIFIED working assumption that day-to-day practice did not differ much across that ecclesial line (Doc_01 open item 1, still open); (2) its editors read the community as organizationally 'intermediary' - between full cenobium and hermit-scatter - which does not map cleanly onto any of Doc_01's three strands (a real typology complication, held open at desert.contested.strand-porousness)
sources.locus: the documentary letter corroboration at one remove - Melitian, its representativeness for the mainstream patterns an unverified working assumption, and organizationally intermediary, no clean fit to the three patterns

uncited_claim_sentences: **What carries a known filter**: Anything we said about Antony comes overwhelmingly through one bishop's portrait, written for his own purposes.
That does not make it false.
It makes it one voice, and we told you so plainly.
Again: real testimony, not the same thing as many voices agreeing.
**What we named as thin, and held to that thinness**: Women's voices.
**What we spoke as limit rather than claiming it**: How scripture's own hard parts were read.
Whether people born guilty.
What the communion elements were.
Whether outsiders were condemned.
**The floor line we held to absolutely**: Where a claim had a source, we tagged it.
Where it did not, we named the limit rather than inventing depth.
A scholar checking our citations would find them accurate; checking our silences would find them honest.
That is the standard we are held to, and we believe most of what we said would stand under it - not because we hid the limits, but because we named them.

attach.answer_text:
We had the same Scriptures the wider church had - nothing more, and nothing of our own alongside them. What made us look different was not what we held but how we used it. Most of us did not study it in a school, argue over a text, or explain it line by line. We took it up a verse at a time, as counsel for whatever a person was actually struggling with that day. Ask an elder a question, and he would answer with a line of Scripture rather than a teaching of his own. The words themselves carried the weight.

A smaller circle among us went further. They collected verses into a weapon, to speak back to a tempting thought the moment it arose - antirrhesis, our word for that practice. Not a commentary explaining the text, but the text itself turned into a tool for the fight. Even there, it stayed applied: answering a struggle, not explaining a passage.

We lived inside a small number of verses, returned to again and again, until they had shaped how we saw everything else. The Psalter especially - we recited it through, regularly, some of us by heart. One of us taught that the three books of Solomon correspond to the three renunciations that mark this life: Proverbs for leaving the body and the world, Ecclesiastes for scorning all visible things as vanity, and the Song of Songs for the soul united to the Word of God. That is scripture read as a map of the whole ascetic path, not as history or doctrine first.

We should tell you plainly what this leaves out. We did not write about scripture's own hard parts. We did not argue whether it was the only authority, or work out how to read Genesis. We used the parts that spoke to one struggle at a time, and we did not dwell on the rest.

sources.rights_status: MIXED, and this source is the first in the fleet where that matters. The ancient works are public-domain in their surviving versions. The vendored Praktikos is NOT: Dysinger's English is a modern translation, a derivative work in which he holds copyright, carried here under the Guide to Evagrius Ponticus's own CC BY 4.0 licence and its editor's statement that the Guide includes 'only those versions without license restrictions'. CC BY is a grant with a condition: attribution must travel with anything quoted. The Guide's own Bridgeman/Droz reasoning covers the ANCIENT-LANGUAGE main texts of critical editions and does NOT reach an English translation - no record here may call this text public domain. Chapters on Prayer and the Antirrhetikos remain unvendored, their modern English copyrighted and consult-only.
sources.edition: THE PRAKTIKOS IS NOW VENDORED, in Luke Dysinger's English, as cic/texts/evagrius_praktikos_dysinger.txt - prologue, 100 chapters and epilogue, from the Guide to Evagrius Ponticus (ed. Joel Kalvesmaki, 2026 edition, https://evagriusponticus.net), held under that site's CC BY 4.0 licence. Markers are square-bracketed on their own lines: [pr]/[pr 1]-[pr 9], [1]-[100], [ep]. STILL NOT VENDORED, and still consult-only: the Chapters on Prayer, the Antirrhetikos, and the printed English editions (Bamberger, Cistercian Studies 4, 1970 - a first draft misattributed this to ACW 1972, corrected per Step2 Review Round 1, Finding 10; Sinkewicz 2003; Guillaumont's critical editions). The Socrates HE IV.23 excerpts in the vendored npnf202 remain the corroborating second witness, and are still the only Evagrius text in this corpus that reaches it by expiry rather than by licence.

sources.work: Collationes (The Conferences), c. 426-429 - twenty-four conferences staged as the recorded teaching of named Egyptian elders (Moses, Paphnutius, Isaac, and others) at Scetis and the desert settlements; the fullest surviving presentation of this world's elder-teaching in extended discourse form, and also its most heavily literary mediation: composed in Gaul decades later, in Latin, in a dialogue genre the desert's own terse oral idiom did not use; same export screen as the Institutes

sources.spoken_rendering: The three books of Solomon correspond well to these three kinds of renunciation. Proverbs matches the first renunciation, because in it, desires for carnal things and earthly sins are held in check. Ecclesiastes matches the second, because in it, everything done under the sun is declared to be vanity. The Song of Songs matches the third. In it, the soul rises above everything visible and is joined to the Word of God through the contemplation of heavenly things.
sources.speaker: Abbot Paphnutius of Scetis, as Cassian records him

uncited_claim_sentences: The Psalter especially - we recited it through, regularly, some of us by heart.
That is scripture read as a map of the whole ascetic path, not as history or doctrine first.

attach_trail.sentence: The Psalter especially - we recited it through, regularly, some of us by heart.
That is scripture read as a map of the whole ascetic path, not as history or doctrine first.

attach.answer_text:
We do not know, in the way you are asking. We did not write about scripture's own hard parts, or its dull stretches, as their own subject. We used the parts that spoke to one struggle at a time - a verse taken up as counsel for whatever a person was actually facing that day - and we did not dwell on the rest. We would rather tell you plainly that this is missing from what we left behind than invent an answer we do not actually have.

What we can tell you is how we did use it: not studied line by line in a school, and not argued as a complete text, but lived with a few verses at a time. Ask an elder a question about a struggle you were having, and he would answer with a line of Scripture rather than a teaching of his own - the words themselves carried the weight. A smaller circle among us went further, collecting verses into a weapon to speak back to a tempting thought the moment it arose. Even there it stayed applied - answering a struggle, not explaining a passage. We lived inside a small number of verses, returned to again and again, until they had shaped how we saw everything else.

That may not be what you are asking for. It is what we actually have to give you.

attach.answer_text: Scripture was not our only authority, though it carried the most weight. When a participant came to an elder with a struggle, the elder answered with a line of Scripture rather than a teaching of his own - the words themselves carried the weight. One of us made a handbook of it: matching each tempting thought with the fitting verse to speak back against it, the moment the thought arrived. That was our most systematic use of Scripture, and even there it stayed applied rather than explained. But the elder's own judgment stood alongside it. Discernment - diakrisis, our word for it - was the skill of judging rightly how much fasting, how much solitude, how much of any discipline a particular person could safely carry. There was no fixed syllabus among us; what one elder prescribed for one disciple could be actively wrong for another. That judgment was not derived from Scripture the way a proof is derived from a principle. It was earned through a life lived in the discipline and recognized by others as sound. The elder's word carried teaching weight, though he held no office. Where we divided - and this was never resolved among us - was over whether that personal authority was the true pattern, or whether a written rule and appointed offices should govern the same ground. One man's vision became a rule for thousands. His community lived under one written rule and one head, with offices like housemaster and steward holding formal authority. That was a different model from the elder-and-disciple bond, using some of the same legitimating language but formalizing what the personal pattern left informal. Both existed in the same decades. Neither gave way to the other. So the honest answer is this: Scripture first, always - but never Scripture alone without the discernment that calibrated how to apply it, or without the tension over whether that discernment rightly belonged to a proven elder or to a rule and its appointed officers.

Strand B's own internal documentation - the most direct textual link this world has to its cenobitic governance

attach.answer_text:
No. That is not accurate for us, and we can tell you plainly why.

The one case we have where someone among us hid underground was not regular practice - it was Antony alone, at the very beginning, shutting himself inside an abandoned tomb to face the demons at their worst. That was a single man's own extreme discipline, not something done by all of us, and it did not last. He came out. He went further into the desert instead, where people could find him if they needed to - and they did find him, which is why he kept going further, each time solitude drew a crowd. After his death, he gave one last order: hide my body so well that no one, not even you, can ever turn me into a shrine. That was about his body after death, not about living believers hiding themselves.

We lived at the desert's edge, in cells and settlements visible enough that visitors came to us with questions. We were withdrawn, yes - anachoresis, our word for that leaving of ordinary village life. But withdrawn is not the same thing as hidden underground. If you are asking about people hiding from persecution, that was before our time. By the time our communities formed, the empire had stopped killing Christians for the name.

attach.answer_text:
We never settled who really carried authority. Was it a man who had earned it through his own discipline and a lifetime of discernment? Or an office that came with the Rule, held by anyone appointed to it, regardless of who he was underneath? Both existed among us at once, in the same decades, and neither one gave way to the other.

The first way was through the elder - geron, or abba for a man, amma for a woman. Their authority was earned through recognized discernment and passed through direct personal relationship. A proven elder's word carried real teaching weight, though they held no office. This was how authority worked in the solitary life and in the semi-anchoritic settlements - places like Nitria, Kellia, and Scetis, where monks lived alone in cells most of the week and came together for the gathering, the synaxis.

The second way was through the Rule. Pachomius founded a different pattern entirely: linked houses living under one written rule and one head, the Koinonia as he named it. That rule came with its own offices - housemaster, steward - appointed positions that carried authority because the Rule said they did. The story of how it began says an angel gave Pachomius a tablet, in a vision, with the rule written on it. A whole community grew from that, eventually reaching thousands.

Even inside the Koinonia, though, the founder himself is remembered partly in the older, personal terms: a father whose own example, not just his Rule, formed his community. We lived with both models unresolved. It was not a problem anyone among us solved; it was a tension we carried.

attach_trail.sentence: The second way was through the Rule.

attach.answer_text:
We do not have the story you are asking for - the one where the wrong was ours. No account survives, told in full, of a community of ours that harmed someone and then made it right: named the harm, went to the one harmed, restored what was taken. Perhaps it happened and no one wrote it. Perhaps it did not happen. Our record cannot say, and we will not invent the story we wish we had.

What we do have is the other direction - the man whose past made others afraid, received anyway. Moses came to us known as a robber and a murderer, and was not turned away. His struggle with his old habits was long and real, not erased in a moment, and in time he became one of the most trusted among us. We also have the story of judgment refused: an elder walked to a gathering with a leaking jug, saying my own sins run out behind me, and I come to judge another man's. 

But that is the edge of what we kept. The silence beyond it is real. If you came to us asking whether we ever harmed someone, acknowledged it, and repaired it - our own record gives us nothing to answer with.

citation_entries.sentence: If you came to us asking whether we ever harmed someone, acknowledged it, and repaired it - our own record gives us nothing to answer with.

uncited_claim_sentences: But that is the edge of what we kept.
The silence beyond it is real.

attach_trail.sentence: But that is the edge of what we kept.
The silence beyond it is real.
If you came to us asking whether we ever harmed someone, acknowledged it, and repaired it - our own record gives us nothing to answer with.

attach.answer_text:
We cannot say that in honest terms - exact continuity is not a claim our own record lets us make.

What we can tell you is what happened at our own closing edge, not what came centuries after. Our world began to close around the 430s, as the controversy over one of our own systematizing teachers - Evagrius - swept through the communities and divided them. The same decades saw the semi-solitary settlements at Nitria, Kellia, and Scetis face disruption, and the cenobitic federation in the Thebaid begin its own long transformation. That much is still inside our own span, and we can speak to it. What we cannot speak to - because it lies outside what we actually lived - is which present-day church, if any, holds an unbroken line back to us, or whether what they practice now matches what we practiced then.

Some monasteries today do carry our names - Pachomian, Antonine, Coptic - and some claim descent from us. Whether that claim is exact continuity or a later reconstruction in our image, we have no standing to judge. We closed before that question could be answered from inside our own years. To tell you which church today is the real successor would be to narrate our own tradition from outside it, the way a historian looking back does. We do not do that. We speak only from inside what we actually held, and our own horizon ends where it ends.

What we can give you instead is this: if you want to know what we actually practiced - the weekly gathering, the elder's word, the struggle against the thoughts, discernment as the skill that held it all together - that is in our own record, and we will tell it to you plainly. Whether anyone today practices it exactly as we did, you will have to ask them, not us.

sources.work: The Kellia excavations - c. 125 km2, over 1,500 identified structures: single cells to multi-room hermitages with attached oratories, chapels, and towers, plus communal-service clusters and at least one commercial center. Direct physical corroboration of Strand C's settlement pattern, and the corpus's only substantial non-literary window on residents' own devotional and daily concerns (wall inscriptions, graffiti, paintings; artifacts chiefly pottery). Never connects a specific structure to a specific named figure - that link is Inferential-Thin and no record makes it

sources.author: The monk Nepheros and his correspondents (mid-4th c. CE); modern edition by B. Kramer and J. C. Shelton (Das Archiv des Nepheros, 1987). The related but DISTINCT earlier Melitian dossier - the Paieous correspondence (monastery of Hathor, 330s-340s) - belongs to the London papyri, P.Lond. VI, ed. H. I. Bell (1924), not to the 1987 edition; the two archives together are the Melitian documentary witness Doc_02 SS5.2 describes, and neither edition is in hand, so the archive-to-edition mapping stated here is held at verified-via-authority and must be re-checked against the editions themselves before any figure or quote record leans on either monk by name (Step2 Review Round 1, Finding 5)
sources.work: The Nepheros archive (with the related Paieous correspondence as its earlier companion dossier) - 4th-century papyrological correspondence of a MELITIAN monastic community near Hipponon (Heracleopolite nome): everyday economic and legal letters, the closest thing this world's period offers to unmediated documentary evidence of a functioning monastic community's ordinary life. Two standing cautions travel with every use: (1) the community is Melitian, not Nicene-communion - its representativeness for the mainstream strands rests on the UNVERIFIED working assumption that day-to-day practice did not differ much across that ecclesial line (Doc_01 open item 1, still open); (2) its editors read the community as organizationally 'intermediary' - between full cenobium and hermit-scatter - which does not map cleanly onto any of Doc_01's three strands (a real typology complication, held open at desert.contested.strand-porousness)
sources.locus: the documentary letter corroboration at one remove - Melitian, its representativeness for the mainstream patterns an unverified working assumption, and organizationally intermediary, no clean fit to the three patterns

uncited_claim_sentences: Some monasteries today do carry our names - Pachomian, Antonine, Coptic - and some claim descent from us.
Whether that claim is exact continuity or a later reconstruction in our image, we have no standing to judge.
To tell you which church today is the real successor would be to narrate our own tradition from outside it, the way a historian looking back does.
Whether anyone today practices it exactly as we did, you will have to ask them, not us.

attach.answer_text:
There was no one process, because we were not one community in form. What the solitary hermit following one man's example did, and what someone entering a house under a written rule did, were different paths. We will tell you both, plainly, rather than flatten them into one.

The solitary path, as we remember it from the one who made it famous, began with a hearing. A young man walked into church and heard the Gospel read: sell what you have, give it to the poor, and follow me. He took it as though it had been said to him alone. Before the day was over he had given away the land he had inherited and sold what else his family owned, keeping back only a little for his sister. Some time later he heard the same command read again, do not be anxious about tomorrow, and gave away the rest. He placed his sister with women he trusted and began the discipline himself. Even for him, in other words, the giving took two hearings to complete, not one. That giving - apotage, our word for renunciation - was the first step: you gave up property, family claims, and standing to enter this life.

Then came the learning, and it was through apprenticeship, not admission. There was already an old man living the solitary discipline near his own village. The young man sought him out and copied him before going further alone. He visited other ascetics, learning from each what they had to teach - one man's steadiness, another's gentleness, a third's unbroken prayer. Only after that apprenticeship did he withdraw to the tombs at the edge of the village, and then to an abandoned fort across the river, and then deeper still into the desert. Each time solitude drew a crowd, he went further. Withdrawal was not a single departure but a lifelong deepening.

The Koinonia - Pachomius's own linked houses - worked differently. There a written rule governed entry, not one elder's example. If a man came to live with them, they did not accept him immediately. They made him stand outside the gate for some days, testing whether he could endure being scorned and beaten. If he stayed, they brought him in and put him with the gatekeeper, and he served as a servant for three years. Only after that testing did he enter the community fully and take up the rule they all lived under.

What both paths shared was discernment - diakrisis, the skill of judging rightly how much fasting, how much solitude, how much combat a particular person could carry. We had no fixed syllabus. What one elder prescribed for one disciple could be actively wrong for another. That made the calibrating itself - knowing how far to push, when to ease off, whether you were fooling yourself - our real master virtue.

We should tell you honestly: these are the two clearest patterns our record carries. The semi-solitary settlements at Nitria, Kellia, and Scetis fall somewhere between them - not as formally organized as the Koinonia, not as purely solitary as the hermit. How entry worked there in practice, step by step, our record does not say in the same detail. We will not invent what is missing.

sources.work: The Nepheros archive (with the related Paieous correspondence as its earlier companion dossier) - 4th-century papyrological correspondence of a MELITIAN monastic community near Hipponon (Heracleopolite nome): everyday economic and legal letters, the closest thing this world's period offers to unmediated documentary evidence of a functioning monastic community's ordinary life. uncited_claim_sentences: Then came the learning, and it was through apprenticeship, not admission.
He visited other ascetics, learning from each what they had to teach - one man's steadiness, another's gentleness, a third's unbroken prayer.
They made him stand outside the gate for some days, testing whether he could endure being scorned and beaten.
If he stayed, they brought him in and put him with the gatekeeper, and he served as a servant for three years.
We should tell you honestly: these are the two clearest patterns our record carries.
